assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Solenoid
items.clue: A wire wound into a long coil of many turns.

items.label: Electromagnetic relay
items.clue: A small current in a coil switches a separate circuit on or off.

items.label: Iron core
items.clue: Placed inside a coil, it greatly increases the strength of the field.

items.label: Electric bell
items.clue: An armature is pulled in, strikes a gong and breaks its own circuit, again and again.

questions.stem: A long straight vertical wire carries a steady current. What is the shape of the magnetic field pattern around the wire?

options.text: Circles centred on the wire and lying in a plane at right angles to it
Straight lines that spread out from the wire, like spokes on a wheel
Straight lines running parallel to the wire along its whole length
Loops that leave one end of the wire and enter at the other end

questions.explanation: The field around a straight current-carrying wire is a set of concentric circles perpendicular to it.

questions.stem: A plotting compass is moved from 2 cm to 6 cm away from a wire carrying a steady current. The current is not changed. What happens to the deflection of the compass?

options.text: It stays the same, because the current through the wire is unchanged
It falls to zero, because the field stops at the outer circle
It gets smaller, because the field is weaker further from the wire
It gets larger, because the field circles are wider further out

questions.explanation: Field strength depends on distance from the wire as well as on the current, so it falls as the compass is moved away.

questions.stem: A student winds a straight wire into a solenoid and passes the same current through it as before. What happens to the magnetic field produced?

options.text: It is weaker, because the current now has a longer path to run
It is stronger, because the fields of the turns add together
It is unchanged, because the current in the wire is unchanged
There is no field at all until an iron core is in the coil

questions.explanation: Shaping a wire into a solenoid increases the strength of the field, because each turn adds its field to its neighbours'.

questions.stem: What best describes the magnetic field inside a long solenoid that is carrying a current?

options.text: Strong at the very centre of the coil and almost zero elsewhere
A set of circles running round the axis, as around a straight wire
Weak inside the coil and strongest just outside the windings
Strong and uniform, drawn as evenly spaced parallel lines

questions.explanation: The specification states that the field inside a solenoid is strong and uniform, so the lines are parallel and evenly spaced.

questions.stem: How does the magnetic field around the outside of a current-carrying solenoid compare with that of a bar magnet?

options.text: It is a set of circles around the middle of the coil, not like a bar magnet
It has a similar shape, with one end acting as a north pole and one as a south
It has exactly the same shape, but the ends of a solenoid are not poles
There is no field outside the coil, so no comparison can be made

questions.explanation: The specification states that the field around a solenoid has a similar shape to that of a bar magnet.

questions.stem: An iron core is placed inside a solenoid that is carrying a current. What is the effect?

options.text: The solenoid begins to produce a magnetic field for the first time
The field grows stronger and stays on after the current is off
The core carries a current of its own that adds to the field
The magnetic field of the solenoid becomes considerably stronger

questions.explanation: Adding an iron core increases the strength of the magnetic field of a solenoid; the arrangement is an electromagnet.

questions.stem: Which observation best demonstrates that a current in a wire produces a magnetic field?

options.text: A compass beside the wire swings round when the current is switched on
A plotting compass beside the wire keeps pointing north when the current is off
The wire becomes noticeably warmer when the current is switched on
A piece of copper wire placed beside the wire is pulled sideways towards it

questions.explanation: The compass responds only to a magnetic field, and it moves exactly when the current begins, so the current is the cause.

questions.stem: The direction of the current in a straight wire is reversed. What happens to the magnetic field pattern?

options.text: The pattern and the arrows on it are both completely unchanged
The circles turn into straight lines pointing back along the wire
The circles stay, but the arrows point the other way round
The circles are replaced by a bar-magnet pattern with swapped poles

questions.explanation: The pattern is fixed by the shape of the wire and the direction by the direction of the current, so only the arrows reverse.

questions.stem: A student is asked to draw the magnetic field of a current-carrying solenoid, showing its direction. Which drawing is correct?

options.text: Parallel lines inside the coil and loops outside it, with no arrows on any line
Parallel arrows inside the coil that start at one end and stop at the other
Closely spaced parallel arrows inside the coil, looping outside from north to south
Circles drawn around the outside of the coil, with clockwise arrows shown

questions.explanation: Inside the coil the field is uniform and along the axis; outside, each line loops back, giving the bar-magnet shape.

questions.stem: Why does winding a wire into a solenoid increase the magnetic effect of the current?

options.text: The field of each turn points the same way inside the coil, so they add up
Winding the wire into a coil increases the current flowing in it
The coiled wire has a much larger resistance, and that strengthens the field
The turns of wire trap the field lines so that none can escape the coil

questions.explanation: Many turns contribute their fields at the same place and in the same direction, so the total field is much stronger.

questions.stem: A relay diagram shows a coil wound on an iron core in one circuit, and a pivoted iron armature that closes contacts in a second circuit. How does the relay work?

options.text: The current in the coil flows on through the contacts and into the second circuit
The magnetised iron core repels the armature and pushes it onto the contacts
The coil heats the armature, which bends until it touches the contacts
A small current magnetises the core, so the armature closes the contacts

questions.explanation: The coil's magnetic effect moves the armature, so a small current in one circuit switches on a separate circuit.

questions.stem: A wire carrying a current is held at right angles to the field between the poles of a magnet. Which statement about the forces is correct?

options.text: Only the wire feels a force, as the magnet carries no current
The magnet and the wire each exert a force on the other
Only the magnet feels a force, because it produces the field
Neither feels a force until the wire is free to move about

questions.explanation: The specification states that the magnet producing the field and the conductor exert a force on each other.

questions.stem: A rectangular coil carrying a current is mounted on an axle between the poles of a magnet. Why does the coil tend to rotate?

options.text: The forces on both of its sides act in the same direction, pushing it
The coil becomes a magnet and is pulled towards the north pole
The forces on its opposite sides act in opposite directions
The current warms the coil, which expands and turns on its axle

questions.explanation: The current runs opposite ways along the two sides, so the forces on them are opposite and turn the coil.

questions.stem: How does a moving-coil loudspeaker produce sound?

options.text: Pressure variations in the air move the cone, which produces a current
The permanent magnet vibrates and passes its vibrations to the cone
The current heats the coil, and the expanding air makes the sound
A varying current in the coil makes it move and push the cone

questions.explanation: The motor effect gives the current-carrying coil a varying force, so the coil and the cone attached to it move in and out.

questions.stem: In Fleming's left-hand rule, what do the first finger, the second finger and the thumb represent?

options.text: The first finger is the current, the second the field, the thumb the motion
The first finger is the force, the second the field, and the thumb current
The right hand is used, with the field, current and force in that order
The first finger the field, the second finger the current, and the thumb the force

questions.explanation: First finger Field, seCond finger Current, thuMb Motion: the three are held at right angles to one another.

questions.stem: In a simple d.c. motor, what is the job of the split-ring commutator?

options.text: It carries the current into the coil, so that a force can act on the coil
It reverses the current in the coil every half turn, so it keeps turning one way
It reverses the magnetic field every half turn, so the coil keeps going
It holds the coil steady so that it turns at a constant rate of spin

questions.explanation: Swapping the connections as the coil passes the vertical swaps the two forces over and keeps the rotation going.

questions.stem: Loudspeakers and headphones use the motor effect. Which conversion do they carry out?

options.text: Pressure variations in a sound wave into variations in current
Movement of a coil in a magnetic field into an induced current in it
Variations in current into a steady push on the air in the room
Variations in current in a circuit into pressure variations in a sound wave

questions.explanation: The specification states that they convert variations in current in electrical circuits to pressure variations in sound waves.
